questions.q: A bank reports 1-day 99% VaR of ₹50 crore. Correct interpretation:
o: On 99 of 100 days the loss will not exceed 50 crore (1-day horizon, current positions, normal markets)
50 crore is the worst possible loss
questions.why: VaR = the loss threshold exceeded on (1−c) fraction of days under the model's assumptions; it says nothing about the size of the tail it doesn't measure — hence stress tests and expected shortfall supplement it.

o: Sunk is irrelevant; opportunity cost is relevant (e.g., foregone rent of owned land)

questions.topic: Capital structure: trade-off vs pecking order
questions.q: Compare the static trade-off theory and the pecking order theory of capital structure. What does each predict about profitable versus unprofitable firms, and which fits Indian promoter-led firms better?
questions.ans: Trade-off: firms balance the tax shield of debt against expected distress/agency costs, implying a target D/E that is re-levered toward — profitable firms should carry MORE debt (bigger shields, lower distress risk). Pecking order (Myers–Majluf): asymmetric information makes internal funds first, debt second, equity last (equity issues are read as over-valuation, price drops) — implies profitable firms borrow LESS because they need less external finance. The two make opposite predictions for exactly the observable: high-profit firms' leverage. Indian context: high promoter control, costly rights issues, thin debt markets but abundant bank credit and collateral culture — pecking-order behaviour (promoter loans, IPO cash hoarding, reluctance to dilute) blends with trade-off discipline imposed by banks' covenant regimes. A full answer concludes that neither is 'true' — leverage policy is a target-with-grammar: a range governed by tax and distress, sequenced by information costs.

questions.q: Why do lenders impose covenants? Classify four covenant types with examples and explain the cost they impose on borrowers.
questions.ans: Covenants mitigate the shareholder–debtholder agency problem (asset substitution, dividend stripping, under-investment). Types: (i) negative pledge — no security to other lenders; (ii) leverage/coverage tests — max D/E, min interest cover, tested quarterly; (iii) distribution restrictions — cap dividends/buybacks until ratios met; (iv) investment restrictions — no capex/mergers beyond agreed limits without consent. Cost to borrower: lost flexibility — rejecting NPV-positive investments that trip a covenant (under-investment), higher effective cost via restricted actions, and 'technical default' renegotiation leverage to the lender (the covenant ratchet: a violation is a free option for the bank). Optimal covenants are tight enough to discipline, loose enough not to strangle — and they are cheaper than collateral for firms with good soft information, costlier for cyclicals (hence revolver-heavy structures).

questions.q: Distinguish total risk from systematic and unsystematic risk with the variance decomposition formula. What does diversification actually remove, and why can a well-diversified investor still lose money in a crash?
questions.ans: Total variance = systematic + idiosyncratic: σ²ᵢ = βᵢ²σ²ₘ + σ²εᵢ. Systematic (market) risk is common-factor movement no diversification removes — in an Indian crash the market factor is the whole loss driver; idiosyncratic risk (firm/industry-specific) averages toward zero with roughly 20–30 equally weighted stocks. A diversified investor still loses in a crash because the market factor itself fell: diversification guarantees the AVERAGE stock's performance, not protection from it. Further nuance: correlations rise in crises (contagion), so even the diversification benefit is state-dependent; and 'unsystematic' risks that are common within a sector (e.g., a power-tariff order) behave like systematic for sector-concentrated portfolios. Exam framing: beta prices systematic risk because markets cannot diversify it away; portfolios price nothing for risk any member could have shed alone.

questions.q: Explain four behavioural biases that distort security valuation or portfolio decisions, and for each name a market anomaly it helps explain.
questions.ans: (i) Overconfidence — excessive trading and under-diversification; explains high turnover and why men trade more than funds should; also 'better-than-average' driver of empire M&A bids. (ii) Anchoring/conservatism — clinging to purchase price or old earnings; explains slow reaction to news (post-earnings-announcement drift) and resistance to re-rating. (iii) Loss aversion & disposition effect — selling winners early, riding losers (prospect theory curvature); explains momentum reversal and volume patterns near round-number price anchors. (iv) Herding/narrative cascades — simultaneous chasing of stories; explains bubbles, sector crowding (IT/Nifty Midcap sprees), and correlated panic selling that raises crisis correlations. Mitigations examiners want: process (checklists, pre-commit rules), outside view (base rates), and forcing functions (reverse DCF, kill criteria). Caveat line: behavioural finance augments, not replaces, CAPM-style pricing — arbitrage limits (costs, short-selling bans, noise-trader risk) let mispricing persist.

questions.q: Compare scenario analysis, sensitivity analysis and Monte-Carlo simulation for a capital project; state what each adds beyond NPV and their key limitation.

All three: risk-adjusted view vs single-point NPV at a risk-loaded discount rate; use alongside real-options logic (option to abandon/expand) for full picture.

questions.q: Project A: NPV Rs 60 crore, 4 years. Project B: NPV Rs 85 crore, 7 years. Both repeatable. Can NPV decide between them? Explain two remedies and when each breaks.
questions.ans: Raw NPV fails when lives differ because it ignores what happens after A's chain ends — the shorter project's cash flow can be reinvested into a repeat of itself. Remedy 1 — replacement chain (common-life): extend to LCM horizon (28 years, 7 A's vs 4 B's), rework the NPV over the common life; correct but ugly with discounting drift and needs true repeatability. Remedy 2 — equivalent annual annuity (EAA): EAA = NPV ÷ annuity factor at WACC; compare per-year value; algebraically identical to the chain under perfect repeatability. Both break when the decision is NOT repeatable: one-shot mine, capacity-limited concession (can't run two A's), or where future repeats face different prices/regulation — then neither chain nor EAA is right; instead use real-option framing or explicitly model the finite repeat horizon. Shortcut for exams: EAA of A = 60/AF(r,4), B = 85/AF(r,7) at given r; a positive EAA gap can flip against the NPV gap.

questions.q: A firm has more positive-NPV projects than funds, and management distrusts the forecast numbers. Explain hard vs soft rationing, the profitability-index method and its flaw, and how a post-audit feeds the process.
questions.ans: Hard rationing: external funds truly unavailable (market for the firm's debt closed, covenants at the wall, information costs block a raise) — the cost of capital itself is not a market-clearing rate, so ranking under the budget constraint is unavoidable. Soft rationing: internal limits (management fear of over-commitment, decentralised risk ceilings) — theoretically the firm should relax and take all +NPV; its persistence is itself an agency signal. Ranking tool: profitability index PI = PV of inflows ÷ initial cost, highest-first until budget spent; flaw — PI is correct only for single-period capital limits and indivisible projects; it ignores scale and multi-period budgets (needs LP/IP programming: maximise ΣNPV s.t. period-wise outlay caps); a big project with lower PI can beat two small ones. Post-audit: compare realised vs forecast, compute NPV error decomposition (industry vs firm vs execution), no-blame culture for honest forecasts, penalise SANDBAGGING and promotion-optimism bias; feeds back as (i) adjusted risk premia per division and (ii) forecast-quality scorecards — this closes the loop making capital budgeting a learning system.

questions.q: Distinguish free cash flow to firm and to equity in construction and in discount rate. When would you value an Indian bank or a leveraged LBO target with which, and why?
questions.ans: FCFF = cash available to ALL capital providers: EBIT(1−t) + D&A − capex − ΔWC; discount at WACC to get ENTERPRISE value, then equity = EV − net debt (+ non-operating assets). FCFE = cash to shareholders only: FCFF − interest(1−t) + net borrowing; discount at cost of equity — direct equity value, no bridge needed. Choice rules: FCFF when leverage is unstable or changing (LBO, turnaround, capital-structure transitions) because WACC is steadier than levered ke, and because debt's explicit flows cancel within FCFF mechanics; FCFE when the firm is stuck at a target leverage and the analyst must handle the financing schedule (bank/financial firms: debt is operations, so FCFE is awkward — these are usually valued on dividends/EXTRA models or EV multiples on adjusted operating profit). For a bank: neither standard FCFF — deposits are operating liabilities and interest is revenue-line; exam-safe statement: value a bank on dividend-discount or excess-return (residual income) framing, and an LBO target on FCFF-at-WACC with explicit debt schedule checks — never force FCFE on a company whose net borrowing swings wildly.

questions.q: Define economic value added and market value added. Explain the adjustment logic EVA applies to accounting profit, and why an EVA-linked incentive plan changes behaviour more than an EPS-linked one.
questions.ans: EVA = NOPAT − WACC × capital employed (or NOPE: net operating profit after tax less a charge on the total capital used). Adjustments to accounting profit exist because GAAP is conservative for tax, not economics: capitalise-and-amortise large brand/advertising spends, add back R&D, reverse LIFO reserves, de-consolidate operating leases into debt (rent capitalised), strip non-operating assets from the base, provision-based smoothing, and adjust for unrecorded financing of receivables via securitisation (the Indian securitised book belongs in capital employed — ECL too). MVA = market cap − equity capital = present value of expected future EVA (the bridge that keeps EVA honest — a stream of EVA must reconcile to what the market pays). Incentive design: EPS rewards P&L-accretive but value-destroying scale (a low-margin acquisition adds EPS if financed cheaply yet earns below WACC); EVA shrinks the payout when capital earns below its cost, pushing divestment, capex discipline, and receivables/inventory tightening — it prices BALANCE-SHEET laziness that EPS misses. Pitfall line: EVA is period-myopic for long-gestation projects unless spends are capitalised (the adjustments ARE the fix) and is vulnerable to accounting games if not independently audited.

questions.q: List and explain five mistakes that routinely make a DCF confidently wrong, and state a check for each.
questions.ans: (i) Terminal-value dominance: TV is often 60–80% of value; check = compute TV share, run g ± 1% sensitivity, cross-check exit multiple implied. (ii) Mixing nominal and real: WACC nominal but cash flows real (or inflation in flows but not in discount rate) — check the inflation basis of g and of the rate together. (iii) FCF double-counting: treating depreciation as an outflow (real error) or ignoring replacement capex (fake growth) — check terminal capex = D&A (steady state) or the growth-consistency equation g = ROIC × reinvestment rate. (iv) Financing leakage: deducting interest in FCF then also loading WACC (or including asset cost in outflow AND in WACC via debt service) — check flows are pre-financing, discount carries the cost. (v) Cycle-blind base year: forecasting off a peak or trough; check = normalise margins to mid-cycle, test against multi-year averages. Additions that earn marks: perpetuity g above GDP forever (impossible size problem), ignoring dilution/ESOP in per-share equity value, and net-debt mistakes — minority interest and quasi-debt (unpaid advances) belong in the EV-to-equity bridge.

questions.ans: MM (1961): with perfect capital markets, given investment policy, dividend payout doesn't affect value — investors can manufacture payouts via homemade dividends (selling shares); value is driven by earning power of assets. Assumptions: no taxes/transaction costs, symmetric info, fixed investment, rational. Counter-1 Bird-in-hand (Gordon/Lintner): investors discount dividends at lower risk than capital gains ⇒ payout raises value (k falls with certainty) — MM rebut: risk of firm, not its split, prices equity. Counter-2 Tax: dividends taxed higher for many investors ⇒ prefer retention/capital gains; India: dividends taxed in company hands (FIT) shifts the balance — differential matters for FPIs/retirees. Counter-3 Client effect: clientele clusters (income vs growth) — changing policy re-prices via demand shifts, not cash flows; also signalling (information asymmetry): cuts signal trouble.

questions.q: Explain when a buyback beats a dividend, the signalling problems each creates, and the effect on EPS and leverage. Add the Indian route (open-market vs tender) tax angle.
questions.ans: Buyback vs dividend: a buyback is flexible, one-off, and return-of-capital — shareholders choose participation (tender), taxing only sellers at capital-gains rates (with indexation at their level), whereas a dividend is forced on all, taxed as income in hands (in India dividend tax sits with the SHAREHOLDER; companies pay no DDT — say this plainly). Buybacks suit: excess-cash firms wanting per-share growth without promising forever (dividends are sticky — cutting them is punished); undervaluation defence (the firm buys at its own discount); EPS boost (fewer shares, and if funded by debt or idle low-yield cash, net income per share rises arithmetically); leverage rises because equity shrinks (D/E on market value increases — MM-I says value mix-neutral but risk-shifts to equity). Signalling problems: dividend increase = management's confidence in durable earnings (the classic signal); buyback signal is noisier — 'cash-rich' positive vs 'no ideas' negative vs 'price-support/takeover defence' cynical; a buyback during a price crash can look like an option payout to insiders ahead of bad news, so disclosure windows (SEBI PIT quiet periods) police it. Open-market buybacks (company trades gradually, price discovery preserved) vs tender offer (fixed premium, instant, pro-rata fairness) — the tax and market-impact differences are the exam contrast. Watch the dilution mirror: a buyback at price ABOVE intrinsic value destroys value for non-tendering holders even as EPS rises — EPS up ≠ shareholders up.

questions.q: A shareholder complains that the company's dividend of Rs 2 per share is too small. Using MM's dividend irrelevance, explain what she can do herself and what frictions make the company's payout still matter.
questions.ans: Under MM (no taxes, no floatation, symmetric information), total return = the firm's investment policy only; the dividend SCHEDULE is separable: she can create a 'homemade dividend' by selling shares (or buying if the payout is too big — reinvest) — Rs 2/share desired ⇒ sell a small slice of the holding equal to the shortfall, or reinvest the excess; the pie size and the share count change, her wealth does not. Irrelevance proof in two lines: with fixed investment, payout = FCFE, so dividend per share = per-share claim of the same cash flows; changing the split between dividend and price merely moves value across her two pockets. Frictions that RELEVATE payout — the answer's body: taxes (dividend vs capital-gains rates differ and change with holding period and residence — in India both largely 10/12.5%-class in hands, but small-saver STCG exemption bands matter), floatation/transaction costs (selling 0.5% of a holding has brokerage and spread), behavioural preference for forced discipline (clients who cannot sell because willpower fails — the 'house money' effect), signalling (the cut is punished beyond arithmetic, so smoothing is rational), and illiquidity/private holdings (no market = no homemade lever). Conclusion: irrelevance is the benchmark; payout policy matters exactly as much as the frictions do — which is why firms 'manage' dividends rather than set them by formula.

questions.topic: Rights issues, bonuses and stock splits
questions.q: Distinguish a rights issue, a bonus issue and a stock split by their effect on cash, share count, capital accounts and theoretical price. Give the cum-rights theoretical ex-price formula with a numeric, and state the value of the right.
questions.ans: Cash: only the rights issue raises NEW money (existing holders subscribe at a discount to market); bonus and split raise nothing. Share count: rights adds shares to SUBSCRIBING holders (non-subscribers are diluted — hence the renounceable variant lets them sell the right instead of losing value); bonus and split multiply every holding pro-rata, leaving ownership percentages unchanged. Capital accounts: bonus transfers free reserves/share premium INTO paid-up capital (ineligible reserves — revaluation surpluses, debit P&L balances — cannot be capitalised); a split only cuts face value (paid-up total untouched); rights increases paid-up at par with the premium above par going to share premium. Theoretical price: cum-rights 400, shares 10 crore, 1 rights share at 250 per 5 held (2 crore new) ⇒ TEP = (400x10 + 250x2)/12 = Rs 375; value of right = cum − TEP = Rs 25 per existing share — the renounceable right is this figure traded. Bonus numeric: 1 bonus per 5 at cum 420 ⇒ TEP = 420x5/6 = 350 — pure re-labelling, wealth-neutral; market reaction is all signal (confidence in cash generation vs the rights message: 'we need money, and here is the discount'). Splits: 10-face to 2-face at 500 ⇒ 100 post-split — retail-access engineering, zero wealth transfer. Examiners reward ending the comparison table with what each says about management intent.

questions.q: Define portfolio drift and rebalancing. Explain the no-trade band policy versus calendar rebalancing, list three costs of rebalancing, and state how an investor's age and taxes should shift the policy.
questions.ans: Drift: assets grow at different rates, so weights wander — a 60/40 equity-debt mix in a bull market becomes 72/28 within a year, silently re-risking the plan. Rebalancing restores target weights. Method 1 — calendar: fixed dates; simple, disciplined, but may rebalance at bad moments and ignores how far drift went. Method 2 — bands: trade only when a weight breaches ±X (absolute or relative); fewer trades in calm markets, acts when it matters, but needs monitoring and can chase in trending markets (buy-back-the-crash risk). Rebalancing is contrarian by construction: you sell rallies, buy falls — behaviourally hard and statistically modest in expected-return terms (it harvests mean-reversion of assets' relative returns, and if markets are trend-driven it can hurt: 'rebalancing is insurance, not alpha'). Costs: transaction costs/brokerage & spread; taxes (selling appreciated equity above the STCG/LTCG thresholds crystallises liability — Indian equity LTCG > 1.25 lakh taxed, debt gains taxed in slab: asset-location in taxable accounts); and information/decision friction. Age & tax shifts: younger can tolerate wider bands and let equity drift (more time to re-risk); pre-retiree tighter bands (sequence risk dominates); in a tax-sheltered account (EPF/PPF-like) band-rebalance freely, in taxable accounts prefer NEW-MONEY rebalancing — direct inflows to the underweight side, selling only when a band is grossly breached. That is the marks-earning structure.

questions.q: Explain four motives for securitizing receivables and two costs/risks it creates for the originator. Distinguish the structure from factoring.
questions.ans: Motives: (i) funding-cost arbitrage — a pool of high-rated consumer/loan receivables can borrow cheaper (AAA senior tranche at near-AA rates) than the originator's own balance sheet (bankruptcy-remote, over-collateralised), so cost of funds falls even with servicing fees paid; (ii) asset–liability duration match — fund long receivables with matching-dated pools instead of short deposits/CP, killing a rollover risk the originator cannot hedge; (iii) capital & ratio management — a true sale removes risk-weighted assets (capital relief for NBFCs/banks; if the structure keeps first-loss, rating agencies still charge capital — exam nuance: 'relief only to the extent of risk truly transferred'); (iv) origination-scale economics — earning on fees and on the spread between asset yield and the securitised funding rather than on the float, so the balance sheet turns over faster (the 'originate-to-distribute' model). Costs/risks: retained first-loss and reputational support (implicit recourse — the 2008 lesson: sponsors rescued doomed vehicles to protect their franchise, so 'transferred risk' came home), plus covenant/liquidity mismatch (trust needs timely collections; servicing failures trigger spread widening), and disclosure/consolidation accounting (retained interests fair-valued; SPE consolidation when control economics persist). Factoring vs securitization: factoring = sale (often recourse) of SHORT-term trade receivables with collection/credit protection as a SERVICE, priced per invoice; securitization = term transaction building marketable DEBT from a diversified pool, priced on tranche credit, no vendor-management service. One line: factoring finances invoices; securitization finances an asset book — via the capital markets.

questions.q: Classify internal versus external credit enhancement and explain, with a structure of your choice, the order in which the first rupee of loss falls.
questions.ans: Internal (built into the pool structure, paid by investors' subordinate cash): (i) SUBORDINATION/tranches — equity/C and mezzanine B absorb losses first, protecting senior A; (ii) OVERCOLLATERALISATION — Rs 110 of assets per Rs 100 of rated notes; (iii) RESERVE (cash collateral) ACCOUNT — months of collections parked, usually the front-most layer; (iv) EXCESS SPREAD — asset yield minus note coupon + fees routed to a notional account before being released to the residual holder (the annual repair fund that catches inflow-year losses before touching principal layers). External (third-party promises): monoline insurance/guarantees (rare in India, common abroad), letters of credit, corporate guarantees from a creditworthy parent (only as good as the guarantor — correlated failure is the catch: parent distress often coincides with pool distress), and cash-collateral swaps. Loss waterfall (e.g. senior 85, mezz 10, equity 5, reserve 4, excess spread 2%/yr): a default loss runs (1) excess spread for the year, (2) reserve, (3) equity C, (4) mezz B, (5) then and only then senior A — enhancement thickness per tranche = what the rating must survive. The exam trap: external wraps move risk, they do not erase correlation; internal layers move risk into the capital structure's own body.

questions.q: Why did SEBI impose a fixed scheme-category framework for mutual funds? Explain its mechanics (core categories, label discipline) and how it protects the retail investor while creating new problems.
questions.ans: The problem: before 2017 funds multiplied with overlapping, re-labelled portfolios — a 'balance plan' here, a 'multi-cap there', the same fund sliding into whatever theme won (style drift), investors comparing apples to renamed oranges, and a daisy-chain of relaunches to reset expense caps or chase hot flows. The framework: fixed core categories for each type (equity: large cap, mid cap, multi cap, ELSS, focused, sectoral/thematic…; debt: overnight, liquid, gilt, corporate bond, credit risk, target maturity…; hybrid: conservative-aggressive, balanced-advantage, multi-asset…) with mandated minimum exposure rules (e.g. large-cap: 80% in top-100 by market cap; credit-risk: 65% in below-AA), ONE fund per category per AMC (no duplication), and the AMFI/TMU unified codes; labels must match the portfolio in substance, changes need notice, exit loads and TER are capped. Protection: like-for-like comparison, category benchmarks for evaluation, no surprise risk migration, predictable liquidity tiers for debt. New problems: categories become CLOSETS — the top-100 cap on large-caps forces mechanical buying regardless of price (index-in-a-box for active money); a fund can be trapped holding bad mid-caps to keep its exposure while the fund manager 'manages around the box'; thematic proliferation returned (every thematic must fit a category — so 'energy' became 'sectoral' — and AMC churn into whichever theme is allowed and hot); and the ONE-fund rule pushes consolidation into larger existing funds mid-holding, creating tax-inefficiency and forced flows. Exam conclusion: categorisation trades style-drift risk for box constraint — a net win for retail comparison, a cost to active flexibility.

questions.q: A client asks: why do most active funds underperform their index over 10 years, yet charging 2% is defensible? Answer with the zero-sum-with-costs argument and name the situations where active management should have an edge.
questions.ans: The arithmetic (Sharpe's subtraction method): gross active returns of all investors net to ~zero before cost (the market IS the aggregate of them); after cost, the average active fund must underperform the index BY total costs — a 1.8% average fee means the average holder loses ~1.8% to the index before any skill, and most Indian large-cap actives have underdone the Nifty 50 TRI over long windows exactly by their TER. Fees are defensible ONLY where the game is not efficient enough for the subtraction argument to bind: (i) small/micro caps — few analysts, low float, illiquidity premium the patient active can harvest; (ii) credit — private negotiation, covenant work, default recovery: alpha lives in the debt desk; (iii) event/thematic dislocations (demergers, stake sales, fraud detection — the active that exits the Satyam early earns its fee forever); (iv) tax and flow management for the client (loss harvesting, holding-period arbitrage) which the index doesn't offer; (v) mandates with liability constraints (insurance ALM, EPF-like glidepaths) where benchmark-matching is not the objective. Practical verdict wording: 'for the large-cap core, index; for the inefficient edges, active with capacity limits — and pay active only where its sources are visible'. Capacity and fee honesty: alpha decays with AUM (small-cap active at 5,000 Cr is a mid-cap fund in disguise); and a fund that outperforms after a fee of 0.4% is the fee you actually keep.

questions.q: Explain how a mutual fund's NAV is computed and how dividends, entry/exit flows and valuation practices distort the return an investor perceives. Give the arithmetic of a dividend adjustment.
questions.ans: NAV = (assets − liabilities)/units: portfolio marked to exchange quotes (equity: closing price; illiquid debt: indicative yields from a valuation committee/AMFI-style matrix, not trade price — the mark is a policy, not a fact), accrued income added, expenses (TER deducted daily from corpus, not charged to the investor separately), flows: money in after 15:30 (T) invests at T+1 NAVs; large-redemption anti-dilution via exit load or in-kind redemption (protects stayers — a point of trust). Distortion 1 — dividend: NAV drops exactly by the distribution (cum NAV 45.20, div 2.00 ⇒ ex 43.20); a 'yield' of 4.4% with a flat year is returning your own rupee — the return that year was zero; ex-div total return = (43.20 + 2.00)/45.20 − 1 = 0.0%; the 'dividend option looks safer than growth option' fallacy rests here (post-2018, dividends are taxed in hands at slab rates, so the growth option's tax deferral is the actual difference). Distortion 2 — flow timing: a redemption paid from cash held for T+1 settlement dilutes the stayers on inflow day and forces forced sales on outflow day; large inflows in a rally buy NAVs the market will mark down (and vice versa) — hence the 'cash drag' tax on all. Distortion 3 — debt marks: matrix yields lag a spread blowout by days (a fund can hold a bond at 100 the market would clear at 92 — the NAV is 'the last time we checked'). Exam use of all this: judge a fund on TRI and rolling-window relative numbers, never point NAVs or dividend yield.

questions.q: Define delta, gamma, theta and vega. Explain, for a dealer long a large call, what each says about tomorrow's P&L and why gamma and theta are the same trade in two currencies.
questions.ans: Delta = ∂V/∂S (how much option value moves with a one-unit underlying move): long 0.6-call ⇒ +0.6 per rupee up, hedge by shorting 0.6 shares per contract (the hedge ratio lives here). Gamma = ∂²V/∂S² = ∂Δ/∂S: the curvature — ATM long options have peak gamma; when S moves, delta re-hedges itself in the RIGHT direction for a long option (buy the dip, sell the rally), which is why long-gamma positions can profit from pure movement (day-trade P&L of delta-hedged position ≈ ½Γ(ΔS)²). Theta = time decay per day (value bleeding as the option approaches expiry), largest ATM. Vega = per 1% volatility: long options are long uncertainty. The dealer long the call: tomorrow = Δ×move + ½Γ×move² − Θ×day + ν×(ΔIV). The key structural line: gamma and theta are the SAME trade priced in two currencies — a delta-hedged long-gamma position pays time-decay RENT for the right to rebalance on moves (long Γ = long optionality = short time; short Γ = harvest theta but own the tail risk); no free gamma in equilibrium (the tension is the Black–Scholes pricing itself). Convexity shrinks near expiry (Γ explodes as ATM decay accelerates — the pin risk zone), and vega and gamma both concentrate in the ATM band — which is why vol traders care about the term structure.

questions.q: Explain index arbitrage between the futures and the cash market, its limits in India, and how it enforces cost-of-carry pricing.
questions.ans: Mechanics: when F > S(1+(r−q)t) (futures rich to fair value), buy the basket (or ETF) and sell futures — the basis locks a riskless gain converging to zero at expiry (sell cash, unwind short); when cheap, reverse: short the basket where borrow exists, buy futures. In India the practical long side uses an ETF basket or Nifty 50 replication (few funds permit simultaneous short baskets of 50 names; stock-borrow (SLB) is shallow, costly and recallable — the reverse arbitrage is structurally weaker than the forward one). Limits: transaction costs (market-impact of 50-order legs, ETF premium/discount to NAV), borrow unavailability and rebate fees, T+1 settlement mismatch (a one-day leg risk that eats thin arb margins — the cash-future legs don't close simultaneously), execution-latency races (arbitrageurs compete down the basis to the cost floor), and the 'squeezed leg' tail (recall of borrowed stock mid-spread converts arb to direction). Enforcement story: because the forward arm is cheap and mechanical (buy basket, short futures, hold), the futures float barely above carry; the discount arm stays wider than premium — the asymmetry itself is a favourite exam observation. Note the expiry-day twist: Indian Nifty futures settle on last-Thursday cash values, so convergence is administratively enforced too — an arb that assumes perfect convergence ignores the 3:00–3:30 quote window risk that has burned desks (that window = the 'expiry pin' risk line).

questions.topic: Black-Scholes inputs and their Indian proxies
questions.q: List the five Black-Scholes inputs, say which are directly observable for an NSE-listed stock option, and explain how each unobservable input is estimated and how errors in them distort a hedge or an ESOP charge.
questions.ans: Inputs: (1) spot S — traded, exact (closing price; mind ex-div dates); (2) strike K — contractual, exact; (3) time to expiry T — exact, but convert trading-day expiry conventions to calendar time correctly; (4) risk-free rate r — use the sovereign yield at matching tenor (91-day T-bill for short-dated NSE options, interpolated G-sec for long tenors) — not call money or FD rates; (5) volatility sigma — the only genuinely unobservable input: historical sigma (e.g. EWMA on daily returns) as the prior, and implied vol from traded options as a market-consensus readout. The circularity trap: pricing an option with the implied vol from that same option reveals the market quote, not an independent value — implied vol is for comparing and hedging, not for valuation. Distortions: sigma error hits vega proportionally (an ATM 1-month option moves several percent of spot for a 10% relative vol error — enough to flip an Ind AS 102 ESOP charge); ignoring discrete dividends overprices calls and over-hedges; using a deposit rate instead of the sovereign rate misstates thin long-dated values. Framing line: BS assumes constant vol, lognormal prices and frictionless markets — all violated in gap-prone NSE conditions, so treat BS as a quoting convention, not truth.

questions.q: A country devalues; its trade balance worsens before improving. Draw the logic (Marshall–Lerner, contracts, pricing-to-market) and say what decides how long the downturn leg lasts.
questions.ans: Two legs: right after devaluation, QUANTITIES are contractual and sticky — exports were priced in foreign currency (revenue per unit in local terms unchanged… careful: export receipts in INR rise, import payments in INR rise) — the DOMINANT effect is VALUE: the same quantities now cost more in rupees (imports) while export volumes can't surge until new orders form — the trade balance (in value terms) deteriorates if import demand is price-insensitive, until volumes re-optimise. The condition that decides direction over time is Marshall–Lerner: net improvement requires Σ(ηₓ+ηₘ) > 1 (long-run elasticities exceed short-run — contracts, certification, sourcing, buyer-switching costs keep short-run elasticities small — that is the 'J' dip). Pricing-to-market: exporters with margin compression (absorb, keep the foreign price) deliberately delay pass-through and reprice later (so export volumes improve before prices — extending the dip); importers in India often pass through fully, shrinking demand fast. Duration of the downward leg: contract tenor and pricing-currency mix (share billed in own currency), lead-lag in invoicing (the same exposure the corporate treasurer hedges for 90 days), supply capacity (can exporters actually ramp?), and confidence effects (if devaluation reads as policy failure, capital flight offsets the trade gain — twin crises). For a CORPORATE on P2 terms: a devaluation's export windfall is an operating call struck at today's volumes; its import-bill cost is certain — the asymmetry IS the J for firms too.

questions.topic: Duration and convexity in bond management
questions.q: Define Macaulay, modified and effective duration and convexity. A 10-year bond (8%, semi-annual) trades at par. Approximate its price change for +150 bps using duration with convexity adjustment and say why the correction goes both ways.
questions.ans: Macaulay duration = weighted average time of cash flows (years); modified = Mac/(1+y/m) — price sensitivity per unit yield change; EFFECTIVE duration is measured for bonds with embedded options (price to a parallel shift of the whole curve, not yield-only), and convexity = the second derivative of price-yield (the curvature). Arithmetic (8%, semi, 10y): MacDur ≈ 7.24, ModDur ≈ 6.95; ΔP/P ≈ −D*×Δy + ½C×Δy². With Δy = 1.5%: duration gives −10.43%; the convexity correction (typical C ≈ 61 for this bond): +½×61×(0.015)² ≈ +0.68% ⇒ ≈ −9.75%. Why both ways: the price-yield curve is convex toward the origin — for a YIELD RISE the curve lies above the tangent line (loss smaller than linear says), for a YIELD FALL the same geometry adds to the gain (gain bigger than linear): the tangent under-predicts in both directions — that is what 'positive convexity pays in both tails' means; bonds with negative convexity (callable, mortgage pools) reverse the sign (price capped at call, falls exceed duration). Portfolio management use: (i) match duration to horizon (the zero-coupon = pure immunisation insight), (ii) when the curve shifts non-parallel, modified duration lies — key-rate and bullet/barbell ladders hedge the shape, not just the level, (iii) convexity itself is a scarce, priced good: high-convexity (low coupon, long maturity) portfolios outperform after big moves whichever way they come, and underperform in stable times (paid in spread).

questions.q: Explain bullet, barbell and ladder portfolios and when each outperforms, plus the carry-rollover decomposition of return and the 'riding the yield curve' trade.
questions.ans: Three shapes against the same duration target: BULLET — one maturity (pure rate play, high convexity vs the ladder? no — bullet has minimum cash-flow dispersion → LOWEST convexity for a given duration; the price falls less on rises and gains less on falls); BARBELL — extremes (3y+30y), maximum dispersion → HIGHEST convexity — wins when rates MOVE (large parallel swings, whichever way, beyond the carry the barbell pays) and when the curve flattens (short leg falls in value less than the long leg gains… check signs: flatten ⇒ long rates down ⇒ 30y leg rallies, 3y stable ⇒ barbell beats bullet); LADDER — even steps (auto-rolling of maturing rungs, reinvestment discipline, the 'default' for uncertain managers; liquidity of near rungs). Return decomposition: total = coupon income + ROLLOVER (a bond 'rolls down' an upward-sloping curve: as maturity shortens, yield declines, price rises — the roll-down return is the slope itself paid in capital gain) + PRICE CHANGE from yield shifts. Riding the curve: buy the 5y when the curve is steep and flat-to-down expectations prevail; earn the 5y coupon + roll-down to the 4y yield as time passes and (assuming no shifts) sell — the trade profits from the SLOPE, not the direction, and dies when the curve re-prices upward at the short end (2022 lesson); it implicitly borrows the roll and owns a short-rate risk if the shift comes early. Exam synthesis: choose shape by a VIEW — barbell (movement/flattening), bullet (directional at your point), ladder (no view, liquidity, reinvestment), and state the convexity argument — 'barbell needs a bigger yield give-up than bullet to hedge the same duration, buying insurance' — that's the marks.

questions.q: In an M&A bid, how is a defensible maximum price derived, and why do acquirers still overpay?
questions.ans: Build the range (2): standalone DCF of the target as-is plus present value of quantified synergies = reservation value; floor from the target market price or negotiated NAV; ceiling = reservation value minus a safety margin - paying above reservation destroys value even when you win. Justify premium (1-2): control premium and synergy capture pass to sellers under competitive bidding; the winner's curse means bidding exactly at value leaves zero gain, so disciplined bidders consciously leave part of the synergy with the seller. List overpayment causes (2): hubris, agency (empire-building, banker fee incentives), winner's curse in private-value auctions, timing and regulatory pressure. Close with safeguards (1): walk-away thresholds, fairness opinions, and synergy haircutting so only downside-surviving value is committed.

questions.q: Explain how ESG considerations enter a financial manager's toolkit through capital costs and risk pricing: sustainability-linked loans/bonds, transition finance and the greenwashing exposure. Keep it finance, not advocacy.
questions.ans: The channel is COST OF CAPITAL and RISK, not sentiment. (i) Sustainability-linked bonds/loans (SLB/SLL): coupon ratchets — the issuer pays a higher coupon (say +25 bps) if it misses a KPI (e.g. emissions intensity −20% by 2030); the pricing works only where the penalty bites and investors monitor (a 25bps ratchet on a 3-year note is a small option to the issuer — market discipline demands credible KPIs at the 'ambition gap'); green bonds ring-fence USE-OF-PROCEEDS (renewables, rail) with second-party opinions (verification = the new audit fee) and a price premium (the 'greenium' ≈ modest in India, real in Europe); (ii) index/covenant effects: ESG rating downgrades reprice bond spreads and index exclusion forces selling (the mechanical cost is in the spread, not the sermon); (iii) transition finance: financing a steel maker's coal-to-DRI shift — the honest version funds DECREASES against a science-based pathway, not only the already-clean (this is the SEBI/Green-Taxonomy work-in-progress point — the taxonomy fight determines which transitions get the discount); (iv) greenwashing exposure — the financial-manager risk: bondholders' mis-selling litigation, SEC/EU-style disclosure penalties, reputational cost-of-capital rebound (the discount is lost AND litigation added) — Indian ESG reporting (BRSR) gives a comparable-data floor that makes misstatements more checkable; end with the finance judgement: ESG metrics that lack verification and contractual teeth are marketing; the discipline of finance is to put the ratchet, the auditor and the taxonomy behind them — then the cost of capital reflects the planet, without the planet reflecting the press release.

questions.q: A CFO proposes to hold more inventory and receivables because 'customers pay slower in a slowdown'. Analyse this under financing-mix (conservative vs aggressive) logic, and set out the cycle-averaging discipline the decision deserves.
questions.ans: Working capital is the cycle amplifier: in a slowdown, DSO lengthens (customers stretch) and inventory turns fall (demand stalls) — the NATURAL answer is not 'more' WC but a POLICY that survives the dip: financing-mix theory — conservative policy funds permanent AND part of the temporary WC with long-term money (low risk, cost of idle carry in good times); aggressive funds temporary WC on short credit (cheap, but rolls the refinancing risk exactly when banks retrench — the slowdown's double hit: needs grow as sources vanish); the match-maturity principle sits between. The decision quality lives in CYCLE-AVERAGING: size the facility to the peak-plus-buffer of the WC/Revenue ratio, not last month's; treat 'customer pays slower' as a PRICE signal — tighten terms, discount early payment (dynamic discounting), factor/pool the receivables (moving the timing, keeping the margin) or hedge the credit (insurance) rather than absorb the float at the firm's own borrow cost; and remember the cash-conversion-cycle math: CCC = DSO + DIO − DPO — every policy 'accommodation' of customers must be funded by an equal tightening elsewhere (payables stretch, inventory reduction) or it converts to a working-capital loan at MCLR to the client, paid by the shareholder. The red-flag: firms calling WC increases 'strategic' while DSO balloons AND their own payables stretch to vendors (pushing the float onto the weakest) — that is vendor-financed stress, and it shows in the vendor list and later in the bad-debt line. Exam conclusion: WC policy should be counter-cyclically conservative (buffer in good years, draw in bad), with cycle-normalised ratio targets and the float explicitly priced — an accommodative WC is a credit product: issue it with terms, pricing and approval authority.

questions.topic: Financial reporting quality and fraud triangle
questions.q: Explain the fraud triangle's three elements in a financial-reporting context, map each to red flags a financial analyst should test, and state how the finance function's incentives (bonuses, covenants) make earnings management a rational-looking crime.
questions.ans: Triangle: (i) INCENTIVE/PRESSURE — the covenants, the bonus threshold, the IPO window, the growth story (a 2% EPS miss from a 10% bonus cliff is a rational-manager motive); incentives turn a decision into a temptation when the gap between 'needed' and 'real' is bridged by ACCRUALS. Analyst tests: accrual quality (cash-flow gap: CFO vs NI divergence over years — earnings up, cash flat = accrual inflation), the ratio of receivables growth to revenue growth (channel-stuffing tell), deferred-revenue movements, one-off gain patterns (asset sales every Q4 = the same trick relabelled). (ii) OPPORTUNITY — weak controls: a concentrated CFO-accounting-team, audit-fee dependence, a board committee that meets quarterly, related-party channels (in India, promoter-controlled vendors) — tests: restatement frequency, auditor rotation & changes, related-party transaction share, governance disclosure (the 'tone at the top' audit is in the numbers of the disclosures). (iii) RATIONALISATION — the language of 'timing differences', 'conservatism in the quarter', 'borrowing from next year' — tests: unusual GAAP elections (depreciation-life extension = earnings without earnings, a straight-line-to-10-year switch is a quarter-saver), policy changes right at the covenant test date (the 'smoking gun' — a ratio just cleared by a just-changed assumption). The 'rational crime' close: earnings management is not always illegal and rarely obvious — it is the firm's choice between a real loss and a delayed loss; the analyst's job is to price the delay (haircut the accruals, raise the cost of equity for low-quality reporting, and treat covenant-driven flexibility as a leverage of TRUTH), not merely to catch the criminal.
